Each binary digit is a bit with a value of zero or one. From the right, place values are 1, 2, 4, 8, and successive powers of two; thus 1101₂ equals 8+4+1, or 13 in decimal. Hex represents each four bits with one digit from 0 to F; D is 13.

A logic gate is a function on bits. AND returns one only when both inputs are one; OR when at least one input is one; XOR only when the inputs differ; and NOT inverts a bit. A truth table covers all possible inputs and specifies the behavior before the circuit is built.

A combinational circuit produces output solely from current inputs and retains no past information. NAND can construct other gates: NAND outputs zero when both inputs are one. Connecting both NAND inputs to the same signal implements NOT.

A combinational gate cannot remember a previous value. A sequential circuit does so using a state-holding element. In the course model, new input becomes the next state at a clock boundary; interpret output with reference to the moments before and after that boundary.

A Bit uses its load signal to choose between storing new input and retaining its previous value. A Register holds multiple bits together; a 16-bit Register means one number with 16 bits of state, not sixteen arbitrary simultaneous operations.

The CPU executes instructions. The ALU performs operations such as addition and AND on data; Registers hold inputs, results, and short-term state. The Control Unit interprets the instruction to determine which data is read from where and written where.

Understanding a processor does not require starting with millions of transistors. Trace an addition: two operands come from Registers or memory, a control signal selects addition, the ALU produces a result, and a write signal updates the destination.

An ISA is the contract between software and processor: it defines executable instructions, visible Registers, ways of addressing data, and instruction behavior. Go or C gives programmers higher-level constructs, which a compiler translates for a target ISA.

x86 and ARM are ISA families with different instructions and conventions; core count, speed, and Cache size are not details of the ISA itself. Two CPUs with similar ISAs can have different implementations and performance. This lesson separates these layers rather than memorizing both architectures' instructions.

In a simple model, Fetch reads an instruction at the Program Counter address, Decode identifies its type and operands, and Execute applies its effect. PC then advances to the next instruction or changes according to a jump condition.

A real processor may overlap these stages and execute them more intricately, but first you must identify the architectural state before and after each instruction precisely. A trace table is better than passive reading: each row contains one instruction, Register values, and the next instruction address.

In this review, explain relationships instead of memorizing terms. The ISA defines instruction behavior; the Control Unit directs execution; the ALU calculates; and a Register holds temporary results. Compare ARM and x86 at this same level, without blanket speed claims.

The CPU does not retrieve data equally quickly from everywhere. Registers, processor-adjacent Caches, and RAM form a hierarchy; nearer levels are usually smaller and faster. A Cache Hit means data was found at the level checked, while a Miss requires consulting a lower level.

SRAM and DRAM are two ways to store bits. SRAM is commonly used for Cache and DRAM for main memory; DRAM requires refresh. Program behavior matters too: accesses close in time or address can create locality and increase the chance of reusing a cache line.

A memory address identifies a data location in a program's address space. A Pointer holds an address; the Pointer itself and the data it points to are distinct. Show both in diagrams to avoid confusing an address change with a value change.

Each process sees a virtual address space. Hardware and the operating system use mechanisms such as page tables to map virtual addresses to physical addresses and control access permissions. Two processes can have the same numeric address yet refer to different physical data.

Virtual Memory is more than extra RAM supplied by disk. The abstraction provides isolation, protection, and mapping; some pages may be absent and loaded through a page fault. The TLB caches recent translations and serves a different role from a data Cache.

CPUs are designed for varied control flows and low latency in general tasks; GPUs execute many similar tasks in parallel for high throughput. Small computations or work dominated by data transfer do not necessarily benefit from a GPU.

A Pipeline overlaps different stages of multiple instructions rather than semantically turning one instruction into several. On a GPU, an SM organizes execution of groups of Threads; CUDA Cores and Tensor Cores are components with different capabilities, and their counts do not directly measure every program's speed.

In CUDA, a Thread is one logical Kernel execution; Threads in a Block can use that Block's Shared Memory and synchronize within the Block. A Grid is the set of Blocks in one launch. A Warp is a Thread execution group; in CUDA's model, a Warp usually contains 32 Threads.

Blocks are scheduled onto SMs; do not assume Block zero always runs on a particular SM. On a CPU, Branch Prediction guesses control flow to keep the pipeline moving; wrong guesses incur costs. Different branches among Warp Threads are a separate concept from CPU branch prediction.

Assembly is a readable representation of machine instructions, but its language and form depend on the ISA and tool syntax. A compiler may remove, combine, or reorder high-level code, so there is no fixed one-to-one correspondence between a Go/C line and an instruction.

In PyTorch, an operation such as Tensor multiplication passes from Python to the library implementation. If the Tensor and suitable backend are on CUDA, GPU Kernels run; Python itself does not execute directly on CUDA Cores. These boundaries help explain transfer time and device selection.

Batch Size is the number of samples processed in one step. Increasing it usually requires more activations and may improve throughput, but this relationship is not linear across all sizes and models. Sequence length or image dimensions can also change usage.

In C, a variable has a type, value, and storage location. The & operator returns its address, and * on a Pointer accesses the value at the target location. A Pointer's type determines the data type the compiler uses to interpret that address.

Unlike Go, C does not automatically manage safety and lifetime for all references. A Pointer to expired data or outside an array can cause undefined behavior. This lesson practices only addresses and valid value changes; the program must not deliberately rely on invalid access.

malloc returns a memory region of the requested size and may fail. Its contents are generally uninitialized. The program must calculate the proper size, check the result, and write valid values before reading cells.

free ends permission to use an allocated region; other Pointers to it also lose permission to read and write. Leaks, double free, and use-after-free are distinct errors. Array bounds are also the program's responsibility; do not trust apparently correct behavior from an invalid execution.

C timing depends on the clock chosen and the operation boundary. A monotonic clock is useful for elapsed intervals where supported; clock() measures process CPU time and differs from wall time. Preserve the metric and tool names in your report.
